title: What is on this iPhone? A first look
lead: An extraction from an iPhone holds thousands of files, and most of them are small databases. This workflow shows how to parse one with iLEAPP, read the report, and confirm important records in the raw database.
time: 2 to 3 hours on the practice data
evidence: An iPhone full file system extraction, or an iTunes or Finder backup, made with your lab's approved tool
answers: What kind of extraction you have and what it can contain
Which device, accounts and apps the report shows
What messages, calls and web pages the phone recorded
Where the phone says it was, and when
How to check a report entry in the raw database
How to read Apple timestamps correctly
need: An extraction folder, archive or backup, or the practice data described in the practice section
iLEAPP, which runs on Windows, macOS or Linux, and DB Browser for SQLite
The backup password, if the backup is encrypted
Free disk space of at least three times the size of the extraction

steps.title: Know which kind of extraction you have
steps.text: A full file system extraction copies the files from the phone's storage, so it can hold the most data. A backup made with Finder or iTunes holds only what iOS puts into a backup. Apple states that an encrypted backup can hold more than an unencrypted one, for example saved passwords, Wi-Fi settings, website history, health data and call history. Check your tool's report to see what you really have.
steps.note: An encrypted backup cannot be used without its password. Write down who supplied the password and how.

steps.title: Record the source and make a working copy
steps.text: Hash the extraction file or the files in the folder, and write the values down with the date, the tool used for the extraction and the phone's model and iOS version. Work on a copy. Keep the original extraction unchanged, in the way your lab requires.

steps.title: Run iLEAPP
steps.text: iLEAPP reads an iOS extraction and writes an HTML report. You can start it with its window, or from the command line. Choose the input type: fs for a folder of extracted files, tar or zip or gz for an archive, and itunes for a Finder or iTunes backup. The output folder must exist before you start. For an encrypted backup, give the password with the password option.
steps.note: On Windows the program may be called ileapp.exe. Use the input type that matches your data.

steps.title: Read the report in a sensible order
steps.text: Open the HTML report in a browser. Start with the device information and the accounts, so that you know whose phone it appears to be. Then look at the installed apps, then messages, call history and Safari history. After that, look at the location items and the photo metadata. Section names change between iLEAPP versions, so use the menu and search box of your version. Make a note of anything you need to confirm.

steps.title: Confirm key records in the raw database
steps.text: Open the original database in DB Browser for SQLite, in read-only mode if the program offers it, on a copy of the file. In a full file system extraction, text messages are in sms.db. In the tables, the message table holds the text and the date, and the handle table holds the phone number or email address of the other side. Compare a few rows with the report.
steps.note: In a backup, files have scrambled names, so ask iLEAPP or your tool which file is which.

steps.title: Convert Apple timestamps
steps.text: Many Apple databases count time from 1 January 2001 UTC. This is called Mac absolute time. Older databases count seconds. Newer ones, such as sms.db on recent iOS versions, can use nanoseconds, which gives a very long number. In SQLite, for nanoseconds, divide by 1000000000 and add 978307200, which is the number of seconds between 1970 and 2001. Check a known message to see that your conversion looks right.

steps.title: Look at property list (plist) files
steps.text: A plist is a file that stores settings, as XML text or in a binary form. Many iOS settings, device details and app preferences are plist files, and iLEAPP reads many of them for you. If an item is missing from the report, find the plist in the extraction and open it with a plist viewer. Note the file path and the key that you read.

steps.title: Try other iOS tools for a second view
steps.text: Mobile Verification Toolkit (MVT) checks backups and file systems for traces of known spyware. APOLLO combines several Apple activity databases into one timeline. mac_apt can also process iOS data. Use them to test what iLEAPP showed, not to take their output on trust.

steps.title: Cross-check and write it down
steps.text: Confirm each important fact from two places, for example the iLEAPP report and the raw database, or two different tools. In your notes, record the tool names and versions, the iOS version, the source file or database path for each fact, the hash of the extraction, and the time zone you used.

artifacts.name: sms.db
artifacts.where: /private/var/mobile/Library/SMS/ in a full file system extraction
artifacts.tells: Text messages and iMessages, with dates, the other party and attachments

artifacts.name: iLEAPP HTML report
artifacts.tells: A readable summary of many artifacts, with links to the source files

artifacts.name: Device and account information
artifacts.where: Property list and database files, shown in the report
artifacts.tells: Device name, iOS version and the accounts signed in on the phone

artifacts.name: Installed apps list
artifacts.where: System databases, shown in the report
artifacts.tells: Which apps were on the phone, and where their data lives

artifacts.name: Call history
artifacts.where: Call history database, shown in the report
artifacts.tells: Calls with time and length. In a backup, only an encrypted one holds it, per Apple

artifacts.name: Safari history
artifacts.where: Safari databases, shown in the report

artifacts.name: Photos database and photo metadata
artifacts.where: Photos library files, shown in the report
artifacts.tells: Photo records with dates and, in some cases, locations

limits: An encrypted backup needs its password. Without it you cannot read the backup.
Deleted data is often not recoverable from an iPhone. A database may keep some deleted records for a short time, but you cannot count on it.
Data kept only in iCloud is not on the phone. A phone extraction does not include it.
Tools lag behind new iOS versions. A new iOS version can change a database and make a parser miss or misread data, so always check the raw database.
A message or a call shows an account and a device. It does not show who typed or said it.
A backup holds less than a full file system extraction, so an empty report section does not prove that the data never existed.
Timestamps can be shown in different time zones by different tools. Always write down which one you used.

practice.name: Digital Corpora: iOS 13 images from Joshua Hickman
practice.by: Joshua Hickman, hosted by Digital Corpora
practice.text: Digital Corpora hosts two public iOS 13 images made for testing and training, one at iOS 13.3.1 and one at iOS 13.4.1. The author's blog post says they come from an iPhone SE and that the phone was jailbroken with checkra1n before extraction. He says each image comes with an iTunes backup, Sysdiagnose logs and documentation, and that the data was created for testing, with many social and messaging apps. The author also posts the SHA-256 and other hash values of the zip files. File sizes are not stated, so expect a large download. No answer sheet is published.
practice.task: Download the iOS 13.3.1 extraction. Check its hash against the author's blog post. Run iLEAPP on it, open the report, and note the device name and iOS version. Find the messages in the report and confirm two of them in sms.db with DB Browser for SQLite, including the converted date.
practice.note: Read the documentation that comes with the data set first. It says how the data was created and how to open the backup. The author's blog post is at https://thebinaryhick.blog/2020/04/16/ios-13-images-images-now-available/
